card.hook: Most people head straight inside Explora, but the building is the star of this photo. Take your first shot before you even reach the door.
card.stand_here: Stand right at Explora in Albuquerque, where the phone icon on the map sits. You're already at the photo spot, so face the front of the building and step back as far as is safe and allowed.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole frontage. If you can't step back far enough, drop to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for signs and details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the slider to make it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the sky stays blue and the walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Soft light in the morning or late afternoon gives the nicest colour on the walls. Midday sun makes harsh shadows and glare on glass, so pick a moment when few people are in front.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold the phone a little above eye level, and keep the Explora building over your shoulder. Walk a few steps left or right until the glass stops reflecting and the walls look straight.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay out of any restricted areas to get a better angle. Photos for personal use are generally fine, but skip the flash where it might disturb others. If you go inside, check the official site first, because photo and entry rules can change.
card.challenge: Take three photos: one wide shot of the whole front, one close-up of a sign or door, and one with a passer-by in the frame to show how big the building is.
card.good_to_know: Explora is at 1701 Mountain Rd NW in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Its colorful dome shows up in photos of the place. Details like signs, doors, shapes and colours make good second and third shots for your set.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at Explora in Albuquerque, where the phone icon on the map sits. You're already at the photo spot, so face the front of the building and step back as far as is safe and allowed.

card.hook: You're in the middle of a desert city, standing by a shaded pond with footbridges, and the earth-toned towers of a Pueblo Revival campus are peeking through the trees. It's calmer than you'd expect, and it photographs well.
card.stand_here: Stand at the UNM Duck Pond and face east, toward the main campus point about 370 m away, so the footbridges and Pueblo Revival buildings fall into your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the pond, the bridges and the trees. Go to 0.5x when you want a footbridge and the buildings in one picture, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for tower tops and wooden beams.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the water or a bridge rail in the bottom third, with the buildings and trees above it.
card.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour is the pick for the pond. Evening is also described as especially beautiful here.
card.selfie_here: Head to the cactus garden beside Zimmerman Library and climb onto the stone steps with the library's nine-story tower behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it so the tower fits over your shoulder. It's roughly 200 m from the pond spot, so check the map.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the sidewalk or lawn by the Castetter Cactus Garden, on the library's west side, and angle the shot so the tower and building sign fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The campus is a working university, and photography may be restricted during official team events or practices, so check the official site before you go. Stay on the sidewalk at the library's west side, not in the doorway, as that entrance is no longer in use.
card.challenge: Take the same bridge shot three times from three different heights, then see which one you'd actually post.
card.good_to_know: The University of New Mexico was founded in 1889, and its main campus covers about 800 acres in central Albuquerque. The Pueblo Revival look goes back to the early 1900s, when president William G. Tight introduced it. Santa Fe architect John Gaw Meem later developed it across the campus.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the UNM Duck Pond and face east, toward the main campus point about 370 m away, so the footbridges and Pueblo Revival buildings fall into your frame.

card.hook: A newspaper contest gave this theater its name, Kimo, which means 'mountain lion'. The front of the building is the real star: a stepped stucco face with a tall neon sign to build your picture around.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk directly across Central Avenue from the KiMo's façade and face the theater. From there you can fit the whole stepped front in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x from across the street. If the sidewalk is too narrow for the whole front, drop to 0.5x, then zoom 2x or more to pick out the terracotta shields above the third-floor windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the front stands up straight, with the neon sign inside the frame.
card.best_time: Morning, roughly 9 to 11 a.m., is the suggested time for the façade. In the evening the lit marquee and neon stand out nicely against the sky, so switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the sidewalk at the corner of Central Ave NW and 5th St NW, where the KiMo sits. Switch to the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and put the façade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on that corner and face northeast, while you stand with the theater filling the view behind you. Check the framing on arrival.
card.rules_and_safety: Central Avenue is busy, so stay well back from the kerb. Inside, personal photos without flash are often allowed in the lobby but may be restricted during performances, so check with the theater's box office.
card.challenge: Zoom to 2x and find the row of terracotta shields above the third-floor windows, then see if you can get one in focus with a bit of neon in the corner.
card.good_to_know: The KiMo opened in September 1927 and is built in a style called Pueblo Deco, which mixes rounded adobe-like forms with tall Art Deco lines. The 24 ft (7.3 m) neon sign is a replica of the original, put up in 2011. The city restored the theater after a fire-damaged spell in the 1970s, and it still stages performances.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sidewalk directly across Central Avenue from the KiMo's façade and face the theater. From there you can fit the whole stepped front in one frame.

card.hook: Picture two white bell towers rising over a little gazebo, with tree-lined walkways leading your eye straight to them. That's Old Town Plaza, and it all fits in one easy frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Old Town Plaza, at the south end, and face north toward San Felipe de Neri Church. The twin towers should sit right above the gazebo.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view of the church above the plaza. If it's crowded, drop to zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the gazebo, trees and towers from close up, or go to 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the towers and facade.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so the church doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the one most guides recommend. For fewer people in your shot, come in the morning or on a weekday, because afternoons get busy with visitors and shoppers.
card.selfie_here: Head to the two replica cannons at the east end of the plaza. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the church and adobe buildings over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: You stand in front of San Felipe de Neri Church on the north side of the plaza, and ask your photographer to shoot from across the plaza so the church and plaza both fit.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is an open public space. Inside the church, photos are generally fine if you're discreet and skip the flash, but services can limit access, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Put a cannon or the gazebo low in the frame, keep both towers perfectly straight behind it, and see if you can do it without a single stranger walking through.
card.good_to_know: Old Town is where Albuquerque began, and the Spanish settlement was recognised as a town in 1706. About ten blocks of low adobe buildings still gather around the plaza, and the church was built in 1793. At Christmas, especially on Christmas Eve, the area is known for its luminaria displays.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Old Town Plaza, at the south end, and face north toward San Felipe de Neri Church. The twin towers should sit right above the gazebo.

card.hook: You know that feeling when a building looks like it's been waiting for you? Frontier is a big barn-shaped place on Central Avenue, with the university campus right across the road and old Route 66 history in the same frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk across from Frontier Restaurant on Central Avenue SE, looking east along the avenue. The University of New Mexico campus should be on your left.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front and a bit of campus on the left. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the corner sign.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright, so the sign and walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the front is evenly lit and the sidewalk is quieter. Early morning or late afternoon is usually softer than midday.
card.selfie_here: Head to the entrance at 2400 Central Ave SE and pose next to the statue of Larry and Dorothy Rainosek. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the statue and the entrance fit behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the sidewalk at the Central Avenue and Cornell Drive corner, across from the restaurant, while you stand by the statue at the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: The street and sidewalk are public, but the restaurant is a business. If you want photos inside, be polite to staff and other diners, and check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and get the building standing straight and Central Avenue running level, then wait for a gap in the traffic for a clean front shot.
card.good_to_know: The Rainosek family opened Frontier in 1971 in a former barn-shaped restaurant building. By 1989 it had grown into the neighbouring buildings to make five dining rooms covering about 740 square metres. Inside, there are more than 100 Western-themed artworks, including several portraits of John Wayne.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sidewalk across from Frontier Restaurant on Central Avenue SE, looking east along the avenue. The University of New Mexico campus should be on your left.

card.hook: Picture a courtyard on a weekend afternoon, with dancers in motion and painted murals glowing behind them. That's the shot here, and it's about people far more than walls.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center courtyard, and face the dancers with the building and murals behind them. Pick a spot at the edge of the audience so nobody's view gets blocked.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole courtyard scene. Go to zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to get closer to the dancers without stepping into their space.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the dancers and slide a little darker if the bright walls or sky wash out.
card.best_time: Go on a Saturday or Sunday, when dance groups perform in the courtyard. Check the centre's events calendar for times.
card.selfie_here: Try the outdoor courtyard, with the adobe walls behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little above eye level and let the walls fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the main entrance and ask a passer-by to step back so the whole facade fits behind you, then ask for a wide shot at zoom 0.5x.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are fine, but ask before taking pictures and treat the Pueblo community as your hosts. Some dance groups ask that their images aren't posted on social media, so check before you share. No flash in the galleries, and the murals are copyrighted, so commercial use needs permission.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the dancers sit in the middle third and the murals fill the background, with not a single tourist's head in the way.
card.good_to_know: The centre is owned and run by the 19 Indian Pueblos of New Mexico. It opened in August 1976 to look after and share Pueblo culture, history and art. The campus also has a museum, galleries, a restaurant and a shop, so there's plenty to see besides photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center courtyard, and face the dancers with the building and murals behind them. Pick a spot at the edge of the audience so nobody's view gets blocked.

card.hook: Picture a row of missiles and military aircraft parked on open ground, with a huge wide sky behind them. That's the museum's outdoor space, and it's a gift for your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Head for La Entrada Southeast, about 100 m south-east of the numbered pin at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the whole building and the open ground in front of it fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the building and the outdoor exhibits together. Use 1x for most shots, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out details on the aircraft and missiles.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the lower line so the sky fills the top, then tap the brightest part of the sky and drag it a little darker so the colour stays.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. The light is softer and the shadows are longer on the outdoor displays than at midday.
card.selfie_here: Try the missile display out front: use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it low so the missile and the building squeeze in over your shoulder. Check the screen on site, since we can't promise the museum lines up behind you. Inside, the Periodic Table granite inlay on the entryway floor, just past the front doors, makes a fun souvenir shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and video for personal use are allowed in the museum, but don't record other visitors without their permission. Flash may be restricted in some exhibits, so check the signs.
card.challenge: Crouch down, tilt your phone up a touch and make a missile look as big as a skyscraper.
card.good_to_know: The museum tells the story of the Atomic Age, from early work on the atom to the Manhattan Project and later nuclear history. It opened in this purpose-built home on 4 April 2009. Inside are 16 permanent exhibit areas, and about nine acres outdoors hold aircraft, missiles, vehicles and the sail of the nuclear submarine USS James K. Polk. It's a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for La Entrada Southeast, about 100 m south-east of the numbered pin at the phone icon on the map. Face north-west and the whole building and the open ground in front of it fit in one frame.

card.hook: Picture a thick, earthy adobe church wearing a pair of tidy Victorian bell towers, like a farmer in a bow tie. That mix is why guides call this front Old Town's most famous photo op.
card.stand_here: Stand in Old Town Plaza, on the open ground across from San Felipe de Neri, which sits on the plaza's north side. Face the church so the whole front and both towers fit in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the whole facade and both towers. Try 2x to pick out the towers and details without walking closer, and use 0.5x only if you're close to the doorway.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the church wall, then slide it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the adobe.
card.best_time: Guides recommend the plaza at sunset, when it looks especially beautiful. Take a quick look at the church front when you arrive, because the light and any renovation work will change how it looks.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the open plaza ground in front of the church, with the facade and twin bell towers behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza lawn across from the church while you pose on the open ground in front of the facade, so both towers fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is not allowed during Mass, confessions, weddings, funerals or private prayer services, so keep clear of the doors around Mass times. Scaffolding or fencing may be up for renovation, so adjust your angle if you need to.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole church, then walk up to the porch and take one close-up of the doorway. Which one makes it into your favourites?
card.good_to_know: The church was built in 1793 and is the only building in Old Town proven to date to the Spanish colonial period. The twin bell towers came later, around 1861, in a simple Gothic Revival style using local materials. It's still a working parish church after more than 200 years of continuous use.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Old Town Plaza, on the open ground across from San Felipe de Neri, which sits on the plaza's north side. Face the church so the whole front and both towers fit in the frame.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: a museum that sits where a truck terminal used to be, with a sculpture garden out front and a building about 158 m across. Bring your best "wow, that's big" face.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum in Old Town, so you're already in the right place when you arrive. For the full frontage, step out to the edge of the grounds or into the sculpture garden and turn back to face the building.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the long frontage and the wide garden views, and 1x for most other shots. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for sculpture details and architectural bits.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap the brightest wall and make the picture a touch darker if the sky or pale surfaces look washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the building. Get there early and you'll have time to try a few spots in the garden.
card.selfie_here: Stand among the large sculptures in front of the main entrance, with the museum building behind you. Or pose beside La Jornada in the sculpture garden, a big sculpture that makes a bold backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the building peek over your shoulder. Neither spot is an official selfie point, so check the angle when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn or concrete paths at the front (east) side of the sculpture garden, facing the building, while you pose among the sculptures so the whole facade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: No selfie sticks are allowed at the museum. Non-flash photography is allowed for personal use, but check the official site before you shoot indoors, as rules can differ inside the galleries.
card.challenge: Find a sculpture you can put in the foreground, with the museum behind it, then take the same shot from three different spots in the garden and pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: The museum was designed by local architect Antoine Predock and opened in 1979. A major expansion by Rohde May Keller McNamara Architecture was finished in 2005, so you'll see more than one era of design. Inside, it looks after art of the American Southwest and the history of Albuquerque and the Middle Rio Grande Valley.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits right at the museum in Old Town, so you're already in the right place when you arrive. For the full frontage, step out to the edge of the grounds or into the sculpture garden and turn back to face the building.

card.hook: Picture a 1946 gas station that decided to become a rock star: shield-shaped Route 66 sign out front, neon running along the roofline. That's the 66 Diner, and it's the easiest big, bold photo you'll take in Albuquerque.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the 66 Diner, at 1405 Central Ave NE, and face the diner's front. You want the shield sign and the roofline neon both in view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole diner in. If the pavement is narrow and you can't step back, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a close-up of just the shield sign.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sign, then slide the brightness down a touch so the neon keeps its colour instead of turning into white glare.
card.best_time: Go at dusk or after dark, when the neon really glows. Some guides say the signs switch off around midnight, and some have been restored or repainted, so check they're lit on the night.
card.selfie_here: Head to the sidewalk in front of the old Nob Hill Court neon sign at 3712 Central Ave SE. It's a 1950s sign that spells out the Nob Hill name, so use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the sign sit behind you. For a postcard-style alternative, look for the 'Greetings from Burque' mural wall in Nob Hill, but check the exact wall before you go.
card.ask_someone: Try Triangle Park, where Central Avenue, Monte Vista and Girard meet, and ask a passer-by to take your picture with the neighbourhood behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the pavement, because Central is busy with traffic. The Nob Hill Court sign is on an active shop property, so just use the sidewalk in front of it.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, park the shield sign on an upper line, and see if you can keep the roofline neon perfectly level. No leaning diners allowed.
card.good_to_know: Nob Hill isn't one hill. It's a neighbourhood along Central Avenue, which became Route 66 in 1937, and it grew up between about 1925 and 1950. Developer D.K.B. Sellers borrowed the name from a fashionable area of San Francisco. In 1947 the district gained Albuquerque's first modern shopping centre, at Central and Carlisle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement in front of the 66 Diner, at 1405 Central Ave NE, and face the diner's front. You want the shield sign and the roofline neon both in view.

card.hook: The first residents you meet at the Rio Grande Zoo aren't even alive. They're metal sculptures standing near the gate, and they make a friendly first photo of the day.
card.stand_here: Stand at the entrance area, right where the phone icon sits on the map at 903 10th St SW. Face the metal sculptures with the gate behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the sculptures and the gate together. Tap 0.5x for the whole entrance, but keep the sculptures away from the edges so they don't look stretched. Then try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for a close-up of one sculpture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put a sculpture on one of the lines, with the gate behind it so people know where you are.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the metal than midday. Arriving soon after opening usually means fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your phone a little higher than usual. Tuck the landmark you like over your shoulder so it fits in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are fine here. Commercial work needs a permit from the BioPark.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole entrance and one close shot of a single sculpture, then crouch a little for a third one so it towers against the sky.
card.good_to_know: The Rio Grande Zoo is the original name of what is now the ABQ BioPark Zoo. It was founded in 1927 and covers 64 acres, so most of your photos will be inside the gates. Once you're in, Flamingo Crossing is the first stop, and Penguin Chill (opened July 2019) has an outdoor deck over the main park.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the entrance area, right where the phone icon sits on the map at 903 10th St SW. Face the metal sculptures with the gate behind them.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the Rio Grande Zoo itself behind the visitor, so I have listed none rather than guess. The only zoo-entrance feature a page mentions is the metal sculptures at the entrance (Rattlesnake, Roadrunner and Yellow Jacket; Peccary and Coyote), per the Zoo Folk blog (https://zoofolk.blog/blog/rio-grande-zoo/). That blog calls them wonderful but does not say they are a photo spot or where to stand with the zoo behind. The tripadvisor page (https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g60933-d526945-Reviews-ABQ_BioPark_Zoo-Albuquerque_New_Mexico.html) mentions a baby gorilla posing at its display, which is an animal, not a landmark. The 'ask someone' spot is also unconfirmed; no page names one. The 'rules' field is empty because no page I found states a selfie stick or tripod rule for this zoo. The National Zoo and Disney rules I found belong to other parks. The city BioPark photo policy (https://www.cabq.gov/artsculture/biopark/about-the-biopark/biopark-photography) says personal, non-commercial photos are welcome and that professional shoots must stay on public paths with all equipment, but it does not mention selfie sticks or tripods, so I did not list it as a rule. Confirm the landmark wording with the user, since 'Rio Grande Zoo' is the older name of the ABQ BioPark Zoo at 903 10th St SW.

card.hook: Floats, horse riders and lowriders all roll down Central Avenue, and you get a kerbside seat with the crowd. It's the best-value photo at the New Mexico State Fair, and you don't even need a ticket for the gate.
card.stand_here: Stand on the kerb on Central Avenue, at the stretch by Alvarado along the parade route. The fairgrounds are to the north, so face along the avenue towards the approaching parade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for floats and the crowd along the kerb. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close shots of riders and lowriders without stepping into the road. Use 0.5x only if you're close and want the whole street.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the float or rider you want, and if the sky is bright, slide the picture a little darker.
card.best_time: Go on a parade day during the September fair, and check the official parade schedule for the start time. Without the parade, the street is much less interesting to photograph.
card.selfie_here: Inside the fairgrounds, try Main Street with the big flag hanging over the street behind you, using the front camera and 0.5x to fit it all in. After dark, stand beside the Ferris wheel on the midway with the lit-up wheel over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The parade only runs on certain days, so check the official site for parade dates and fairgrounds entry details before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a horse rider and a lowrider in the same frame, with a few spectators in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The fair began in 1881, but the present grounds were built in 1936-38 with Works Progress Administration funding. The first fair here was in 1938, and several of the original adobe buildings still stand. You'll also find a boxcar from the 1949 Merci Train, a gift from France.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the kerb on Central Avenue, at the stretch by Alvarado along the parade route. The fairgrounds are to the north, so face along the avenue towards the approaching parade.

I could not check the fairgrounds layout or confirm current locations on a map, so verify the Main Street and Ferris wheel positions before relying on them.

card.hook: Here's a ballpark where the best free photos happen outside the gates. Take a slow lap and you'll get bright Southwestern stucco with the Sandia Mountains popping up behind it.
card.stand_here: Start at the main gates on Avenida Cesar Chavez SE, right where the phone icon sits. Face the stucco walls so the mountains sit behind the stadium, then keep walking round the outside.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x when you're close to the walls, so the stucco frontage and the sky both fit. Use 1x for general views with the mountains behind. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the Sandia Mountains in closer to the stadium.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the stadium wall on the lower third, with mountains and sky above. Then tap the wall and slide it a little darker so the sky and mountains keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go around sunset, when the Sandia Mountains turn pink behind the stadium. Games run through the summer, so check the schedule if you want a ballpark view at that hour.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the entrance plaza at the front of the park, with the colourful glass tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low, so the tower stays over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand back on the entrance plaza, far enough to fit the glass tower and the whole front in the frame, while you stand in front of the tower.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is free to walk around, but views from inside the ballpark generally need a game ticket. If you photograph players close up, skip the flash.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the building's lines point straight at the mountains, then get the wall, the lines and the peaks all in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The ballpark holds 13,279 people, and the field sits above 5,100 feet (1,555 m), which is why the ball carries so well. Inside, statues of Homer, Marge, Lisa and Bart Simpson stand on the concourse. A 2001 Simpsons episode about the Springfield Isotopes inspired the real team's name.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the main gates on Avenida Cesar Chavez SE, right where the phone icon sits. Face the stucco walls so the mountains sit behind the stadium, then keep walking round the outside.

card.hook: Two bronze dinosaurs stand guard at the door of this Albuquerque museum, and they are far better photo buddies than most people you'll meet on holiday. Spike and Alberta never blink, never move, and make anyone next to them look tiny.
card.stand_here: Head to the museum entrance, just outside Old Town, where the bronze dinosaurs are. The phone icon sits in the middle of the museum's outline, so follow the Navigate buttons and then walk to the front door. Choose the side with the cleanest background and face the dinosaurs with the building behind them.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a friend or family member standing beside a dinosaur. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you want the statue and the building in one frame, and keep people away from the edges because things stretch out there.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the dinosaur on one line, tap its face to sharpen it, and slide the picture a touch darker if the sky is bright so the bronze keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when the low sun makes the bronze look warmer. Mid-afternoon sun can throw hard shadows over the statues.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie outside the entrance, right beside the Spike and Alberta statues. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck a dinosaur over your shoulder. If you'd like a second one, Stan the T. rex skeleton is just inside the main foyer, but he's indoors, so the building won't be behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the tail of the bronze dinosaur, so the museum front fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside can differ between galleries and exhibits, and flash may be restricted, so look for signs or ask at the desk.
card.challenge: Pose so it looks like Spike or Alberta is guarding you, then take a second shot where you're guarding them.
card.good_to_know: The two bronzes are a Pentaceratops called Spike and an Albertosaurus called Alberta, made by artist David A. Thomas and put in place in 1985 and 1987. The museum opened on 11 January 1986, partly so New Mexico's dinosaur fossils could stay in the state. Outside you'll also find "A Walk Through New Mexico", a landscape display of the state's geology and terrain that makes a calmer wide shot.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the museum entrance, just outside Old Town, where the bronze dinosaurs are. The phone icon sits in the middle of the museum's outline, so follow the Navigate buttons and then walk to the front door. Choose the side with the cleanest background and face the dinosaurs with the building behind them.

card.hook: From the street, The Pit looks like a low, wide building that never grew up. Surprise: most of it is hiding underground.
card.stand_here: Stand at University Stadium, on the east side of The Pit across University Blvd SE, and face west. The arena is about 357 m away to the west, a short walk, and you'll see the glass tower and curved roof of the east facade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole east facade, glass tower and curved roof into one shot. Then try 1x for a tidier crop, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details like the glass tower or the roof edge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the glass tower up with a vertical line so the building doesn't lean, and tap the glass facade, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: The east-facing front will probably catch morning sun, though that's a guess rather than a promise. Event days can be busy, so check the arena's schedule first.
card.selfie_here: Our pick is beside the two wolf statues outside the main entrance. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the arena behind you. It's not an official selfie spot, just a fun Lobo-themed foreground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk across University Blvd from University Stadium, pointing their phone at the east facade, while you stand in front of the arena with the glass tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Event days and entry rules at University Stadium and the arena may limit access, so check the official site before you go. The area around The Pit is described as well lit with plenty of security.
card.challenge: Get the curved roof, the glass tower and a slice of sky into one frame with the lines dead straight, then walk to the wolves and give them a starring role.
card.good_to_know: The Pit opened in 1966 as University Arena, but students were calling it "The Pit" before the first game. The playing floor sits 37 feet (11 m) below street level. The roof was built first, just above street level, and the bowl was dug out underneath it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at University Stadium, on the east side of The Pit across University Blvd SE, and face west. The arena is about 357 m away to the west, a short walk, and you'll see the glass tower and curved roof of the east facade.
